idea_1789617458_45cdd1.desc: A mobile-friendly web application where users can log daily meals and physical activity. Uses ML to estimate calories and recommend personalized meal plans.
tech_stack: Flask 2.2 (Python) with Flask‑RESTful for API endpoints
PostgreSQL (Render free tier) – use SQLAlchemy ORM; SQLite for local dev
USDA FoodData Central API (free) for nutrition data; optional HuggingFace inference API for pre‑trained calorie estimator
GitHub Actions CI/CD → Docker build → Deploy on Render (free tier) ; containerization with Docker
Jest + React Testing Library for frontend unit/integration; Pytest + pytest‑cov for backend; GitHub Actions runs test suites on each push
idea_1789617458_45cdd1.title: Smart Health Tracker & AI Diet Assistant

strengths: Well‑defined user problem (meal logging + personalized diet advice) that aligns with existing health‑tech demand
Abundant free resources: USDA FoodData Central, open‑source nutrition APIs, and pre‑trained ML models for calorie estimation
Team shows solid DevOps (4/5) and version‑control (git 4/5) capabilities, facilitating CI/CD and deployment
bottlenecks: Accurate calorie estimation is non‑trivial; building a custom image/text recognizer from scratch would exceed the timeline
Web‑development and ML integration experience is only moderate (3/5); the team must lock down a lightweight stack (e.g., Flask/Django + React) early to avoid scope creep

scopeReport.problemStatement: Many individuals want to monitor their daily caloric intake and physical activity but find existing solutions either too manual or reliant on costly APIs and complex image‑based food recognition. This project delivers a lightweight, mobile‑friendly web application that lets users log meals and activities, automatically estimates calories from textual food descriptions using a pre‑trained model, and generates a personalized daily meal plan based on the user's calorie goal.
objectives: Develop a responsive web interface for users to record meals and physical activities.
Integrate a lightweight machine‑learning component that estimates calories from textual food entries using publicly available nutrition data.
Create a rule‑based recommendation engine that produces a simple personalized meal plan aligned with the user's daily calorie target.
inScope: Frontend built with React (or plain JavaScript) optimized for mobile browsers.
Backend API using Flask or Django with user registration/login and CRUD endpoints for meals and activities.
Calorie estimation using a pre‑trained model or a simple regression trained on USDA FoodData Central dataset.
Rule‑based daily meal‑plan generator that respects a user‑defined calorie goal.
Data persistence with SQLite (or PostgreSQL free tier).
Automated CI/CD pipeline with GitHub Actions and deployment to a free cloud host (e.g., Render, Heroku).
Basic unit and integration tests for core functionality.
outOfScope: Image‑based food recognition or custom deep‑learning models trained from scratch.
Integration with wearable devices, third‑party fitness APIs, or real‑time activity tracking.
Comprehensive macro‑ and micronutrient analysis beyond total calories.
Multi‑language UI, accessibility compliance, or production‑grade security (OAuth, GDPR).
Scalable architecture for thousands of concurrent users.
scopeReport.targetUsers: Health‑conscious adults, college students, or anyone who wants a simple, low‑effort way to track calories and receive basic personalized diet suggestions via a web browser.
keyDeliverables: Fully documented source code repository (Git) with README and setup instructions.
Deployed web application accessible via a public URL.
Technical report describing system architecture, data pipeline, ML model selection, and recommendation logic.
User guide illustrating how to log meals, view calorie estimates, and interpret the suggested meal plan.
assumptions: Users will provide food entries as free‑text descriptions (e.g., "2 eggs, 1 slice toast").
Calorie estimation can rely on publicly available nutrition datasets without needing proprietary data.
Team members can allocate ~20 hours per week each over the 60‑day period.
The project will be hosted on free‑tier cloud services with limited traffic.
No regulatory compliance (e.g., HIPAA) is required for the prototype.
constraints: Team size limited to three members with moderate skill levels in Python, JavaScript, web development, and DevOps.
Total project duration is 60 days (≈9 weeks).
Only free or open‑source tools and services may be used.
Scope must avoid custom image processing or large‑scale ML training.

strengths: Well‑defined user problem (meal logging + personalized diet advice) that aligns with existing health‑tech demand
Abundant free resources: USDA FoodData Central, open‑source nutrition APIs, and pre‑trained ML models for calorie estimation
Team shows solid DevOps (4/5) and version‑control (git 4/5) capabilities, facilitating CI/CD and deployment
bottlenecks: Accurate calorie estimation is non‑trivial; building a custom image/text recognizer from scratch would exceed the timeline
Web‑development and ML integration experience is only moderate (3/5); the team must lock down a lightweight stack (e.g., Flask/Django + React) early to avoid scope creep

recommendedStack.backend: Flask 2.2 (Python) with Flask‑RESTful for API endpoints
recommendedStack.database: PostgreSQL (Render free tier) – use SQLAlchemy ORM; SQLite for local dev
recommendedStack.apis: USDA FoodData Central API (free) for nutrition data; optional HuggingFace inference API for pre‑trained calorie estimator
recommendedStack.devops: GitHub Actions CI/CD → Docker build → Deploy on Render (free tier) ; containerization with Docker
recommendedStack.testing: Jest + React Testing Library for frontend unit/integration; Pytest + pytest‑cov for backend; GitHub Actions runs test suites on each push

reasoning: Step 1: The Feasibility Report gives an overall score of 72% and a verdict of 'Feasible with Guidance', indicating the project can succeed if the stack stays lightweight; therefore we avoid heavyweight frameworks and choose simple, well‑documented tools.

Step 2: Scope constraints (team of 3, 60‑day timeline, moderate skill levels) demand a minimal learning curve; React with Vite and Flask are explicitly listed as in‑scope options and are easier to pick up than full‑stack Django or Angular.

Step 3: In‑scope features require a responsive mobile web UI and CRUD APIs; React 18 provides component‑based UI and Vite gives fast hot‑module reload, while Flask‑RESTful lets us expose the needed endpoints quickly.

Step 4: Student skill profile shows Python and JavaScript at 3/5 and DevOps at 4/5; Flask leverages their Python knowledge, and the team’s strong DevOps rating supports Docker and GitHub Actions without steep new learning.

Step 5: The Feasibility bottleneck is accurate calorie estimation; by using the USDA FoodData Central API and a pre‑trained model hosted on HuggingFace we sidestep custom training, keeping the ML component lightweight and within the timeline.

alternatives.tradeoff: Lower learning overhead but loses component reusability and modern state management that React provides.
More built‑in admin and auth features, but adds complexity and longer setup time for a small team.

alternatives.alternative: SQLite (file‑based) for both dev and production
alternatives.tradeoff: Zero‑config and easy for prototyping, but does not scale to concurrent users and lacks server‑side features of PostgreSQL.

alternatives.alternative: Heroku free dyno with GitHub Actions
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler deployment workflow, but free dynos sleep after inactivity and have limited monthly hours.

techStackReport.justification: Both upstream reports stress a lightweight, free‑tier stack that matches the team's moderate Python/JS skills and tight 60‑day schedule; the chosen React‑Flask‑PostgreSQL‑Render combo satisfies all in‑scope requirements while mitigating the ML bottleneck via external nutrition APIs.
learningResources: USDA FoodData Central API Guide – https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/api-guide.html
GitHub Actions CI/CD for Python & Node – https://docs.github.com/en/actions

milestones.title: Initialize repository, CI/CD, and scaffold
milestones.description: Set up version control, continuous integration, containerization, and the basic skeleton for both backend (Flask) and frontend (React Vite). Establish coding standards and document the high‑level architecture.
deliverables: GitHub repository with README, CODE_OF_CONDUCT, and CONTRIBUTING guidelines
Dockerfile + docker‑compose for dev environment
GitHub Actions workflow that builds Docker images and runs unit tests (pytest & Jest)
Flask project scaffold with placeholder auth routes
React Vite project scaffold with a placeholder home page
acceptanceCriteria: Repository is public (or faculty‑approved private) and contains the listed files
CI pipeline runs on every push and reports "All checks passed"
Docker images build without errors locally
Backend server starts and returns 200 on '/'
Frontend loads in a browser and displays the placeholder page

milestones.title: User management, data model, and CRUD APIs
milestones.description: Implement secure user registration/login with JWT, design PostgreSQL schema, create SQLAlchemy models, and expose RESTful endpoints for meals and activities. Wrap USDA FoodData Central API for nutrition lookup.
deliverables: User registration & login endpoints with JWT authentication
SQLAlchemy models + Alembic migrations for users, meals, activities
CRUD API routes: /meals, /activities (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE)
Utility module that queries USDA FoodData API and caches results
Backend unit‑test suite with ≥80 % coverage
acceptanceCriteria: All endpoints return correct HTTP status codes and JSON payloads
Authenticated requests succeed; unauthenticated requests are rejected
Database migrations run cleanly on both SQLite (dev) and PostgreSQL (Render)
CI shows all backend tests passing and coverage ≥80 %
Swagger/OpenAPI spec generated and accessible

milestones.title: Integrate pre‑trained calorie estimator and rule‑based planner
milestones.description: Leverage a HuggingFace inference endpoint (or a simple regression model trained on USDA data) to estimate calories from free‑text food descriptions. Build a deterministic planner that assembles a daily meal plan meeting the user’s calorie goal.
deliverables: /estimate endpoint that accepts a text description and returns estimated calories
Training script (if regression) and model artifact stored in the repo
Rule‑based planner service that generates a 3‑meal plan respecting the user’s target calories
Integration tests covering estimator and planner logic
Documentation of model selection, data preprocessing, and planner algorithm
acceptanceCriteria: Estimator returns values within ±10 % of ground‑truth for a 10‑item validation set
Planner produces a meal list whose total calories are within ±5 % of the user’s goal
Endpoints are documented in the OpenAPI spec
All new tests pass in CI and overall coverage stays ≥80 %
Performance of the estimator call ≤ 1 s per request in the dev environment

milestones.title: Build mobile‑friendly UI and connect to backend
milestones.description: Develop React components for authentication, meal/activity logging, calorie display, and daily meal‑plan view. Wire up API service layer, implement client‑side validation, and ensure responsive design across common mobile screen sizes.
deliverables: Login & registration pages with JWT storage (httpOnly cookie or localStorage)
Meal entry form that calls /estimate and shows estimated calories
Activity logging page with CRUD operations
Daily meal‑plan dashboard showing generated plan and total calories
End‑to‑end test suite (Cypress or React Testing Library) covering main user flows
acceptanceCriteria: All UI pages render without console errors and are responsive (mobile breakpoint ≤ 480 px)
Data entered in the UI persists in the backend and is reflected on refresh
Calorie estimation updates in real time after meal entry
Generated meal plan matches the backend planner output
E2E tests run in CI and pass; overall frontend test coverage ≥80 %

milestones.title: Production deployment, final reporting, and faculty demo
milestones.description: Containerize the full stack, deploy to Render (or equivalent), finalize all documentation, and prepare the technical report and demo presentation for faculty evaluation.
deliverables: Docker‑Compose production configuration and Render deployment scripts
Live public URL with HTTPS and functional end‑to‑end workflow
Comprehensive README with setup, deployment, and usage instructions
Technical report (≈10 pages) covering architecture, data pipeline, model choice, recommendation logic, and testing results
Demo video (5‑min) and slide deck for faculty presentation
acceptanceCriteria: Application is reachable at the public URL and all core features work without manual environment tweaks
CI pipeline builds and pushes Docker images to Render on every merge to main
README allows a new developer to clone, run, and test the app in ≤30 min
Technical report submitted via the faculty portal and passes plagiarism check
Faculty demo scheduled and successfully showcases all milestone deliverables

trackingReport.sprintMethodology: Two‑week Scrum sprints with a fixed backlog, daily stand‑ups (15 min), sprint review/demo and retrospective at the end of each sprint, and a lightweight Kanban board to visualize progress.
immediateActionItems: Create the GitHub repository, add all three team members, and set up branch protection rules.
Populate the initial project backlog in a Kanban board (e.g., GitHub Projects) and define user stories for each milestone.
Configure GitHub Actions with a basic workflow that runs linting and placeholder tests for both backend and frontend.
facultyCheckpoints: Checkpoint 1: End of Week 2 – Review repository setup, CI/CD pipeline, and initial project scaffolding.
Checkpoint 2: End of Week 4 – Demonstrate functional user authentication, database schema, and CRUD APIs.
Checkpoint 3: End of Week 8 – Live demo of the integrated UI, calorie estimation, and meal‑plan generation on a staging URL.
Checkpoint 4: End of Week 9 – Final presentation, deployed production URL, and submission of the technical report.
